items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: Jefferson's draft Declaration condemned slavery — Congress cut it
items.claim: What happened to the anti-slavery clause in Jefferson's 1776 Declaration draft?

options.text: Jefferson included a passage blaming the slave trade on George III ('he has waged cruel war against human nature itself'); the Continental Congress removed it under pressure from South Carolina and Georgia
It was added later by Adams and Franklin
It was kept but ignored in practice

items.reveal:
Jefferson's draft (June 1776) called slavery 'execrable commerce' and blamed George III for it — a strained legal claim, since the colonists themselves operated the trade. Jefferson himself enslaved over 600 people across his life.

The Continental Congress's edits removed the passage on 4 July. Jefferson later wrote his autobiography accusing 'our Southern brethren' of the cut, though Northern delegates also supported removal.

The 1808 expiration of the constitutional protection of the trade (article I section 9) finally allowed federal abolition of the Atlantic slave trade — though domestic slavery continued until the Thirteenth Amendment (1865).
items.why: Founding documents are political compromises. The American Revolution's promise of liberty had a slavery-shaped hole written into it by deliberate editorial decision — the contradiction that produced the Civil War 85 years later.

items.title: Naseby (1645) was won by the New Model Army
items.claim: What was the Battle of Naseby?

options.text: On 14 June 1645, Parliament's New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax (with Oliver Cromwell commanding cavalry) decisively defeated Charles I's army in Northamptonshire — capturing his correspondence with foreign powers and ending hope of Royalist victory
A naval engagement in the English Channel
The first battle of the war (1642)

items.reveal:
The New Model Army had been formed by ordinance in February 1645 — the first national professional army, of around 22,000 men. Naseby was its first major test. Parliament's forces of around 14,000 defeated the king's 9,000.

The king's baggage train was captured, including his correspondence — letters showing he was negotiating with Irish Catholics and foreign Catholic powers for military aid. The 'King's Cabinet Opened' (published July 1645) destroyed remaining sympathy in Parliament.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in May 1646. He was handed to Parliament in 1647, tried for treason in January 1649, and executed on 30 January.
items.why: Single battles can decide wars. Naseby ended the Royalist field army; the king's captured letters ended any chance of negotiated settlement. The two together made the regicide of 1649 possible.
